834.title: The crow in Babylon
834.hook: a crow is prized in a foreign land until a peacock arrives (Jataka 339)
834.howItsDone: The Pali texts name eight worldly conditions that keep the world turning: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. Teachers use tales like this one to show praise leaving as easily as it came.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a hare, a fruit on a palm leaf, and the lion who went back to check. Your line: check first. Today, a new week, and a long voyage by sea.

In the land of Baveru, the tale says, there were no birds at all. Some readers take Baveru to be Babylon. Into this birdless country sail merchants from far away, with a crow aboard their ship. An ordinary black crow. The people of Baveru crowd the dock to see it. They have never seen anything like it, and they can't stop talking about it.
screen: `A LAND WITH NO BIRDS.` → `MERCHANTS ARRIVE BY SHIP.` → `AN ORDINARY BLACK CROW.`

segments.voice: First, the crow's glory. The people of Baveru praise everything about it: the gloss of its feathers, its beak, its voice. They buy it for a high price, keep it in a fine cage, and feed it meat and fruit. For a while, a plain crow is the talk of the country. Second, the peacock. On a later voyage, the merchants bring a peacock, trained to cry out at a snap of the fingers and dance at a clap of the hands. The people are dazzled. It sells for far more than the crow ever did. Third, the crow forgotten. From that day nobody brings the crow its meat and fruit. It flies off, and the tale leaves it scratching for scraps in a rubbish heap. The verse says it plainly: until the peacock came, they honored the crow. Fourth, reading it. The crow did nothing wrong. It never changed: a crow when they praised it, and a crow when they forgot it. It was prized because nothing else was there, and dropped the moment something brighter arrived. So the praise was never quite about the crow. Praise that depends on there being no peacock was always borrowed. Being ordinary was never the loss; the praise was only ever a season.
screen: `THE CROW IN A FINE CAGE.` · `A PEACOCK THAT DANCES.` · `NOBODY FEEDS THE CROW.` · `IT NEVER CHANGED.` · then, large: `THEN THE PEACOCK CAME.`

segments.voice: Sit as an ordinary person on an ordinary day, with no achievement to admire and no audience. Feel the plain things, your weight on the seat, the air at your nose, a sound somewhere in the room, and see whether it's restful that none of it is special. Let the peacocks dance somewhere else.
Mayura. Peacock: the bird whose arrival ended a plain crow's glory in a land with no birds, in a Jataka tale. Today's word.
Your line: then the peacock came. The crow was a good crow before Baveru, and after. That's day eight hundred thirty-four.

835.title: The jackal's judgment
835.hook: two otters quarrel over a fish; the jackal judge takes the middle (Jataka 400)
835.howItsDone: The monastic code, the Vinaya, sets out ways for monks and nuns to settle disputes within the community themselves, and this tale's frame is about a dispute settled badly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the crow in Babylon, prized until the mayura, the peacock, arrived. Your line: then the peacock came. Today, two otters and one very large fish.

On a riverbank, two otters are hunting together, one working the deep water, one along the shore. The deep-water otter bites into a huge fish, so strong it starts dragging him under. He calls out, and his partner rushes in. Together they wrestle it onto the bank, and lie there panting, very pleased. Then one of them says: so, how do we split it? That's where the Dabbhapuppha Jataka turns.
screen: `TWO OTTERS HUNTING.` → `A FISH TOO BIG FOR ONE.` → `HOW DO WE SPLIT IT?`

segments.voice: First, the teamwork. Neither otter could have landed that fish alone; it took one in the deep and one on the shore. Second, the quarrel. Now each is sure he deserves the better share. One caught it; the other saved him. Neither will give an inch, and the argument goes round and round. Third, the judge. A jackal comes down to drink, and the otters, tired of arguing, ask him to settle it. He's happy to oblige. He gives the tail to the otter who worked the shore, and the head to the otter who went into the deep. The whole middle, the meat of the fish, he takes for himself as his fee for judging. Off he trots, leaving the otters staring at a head and a tail. Fourth, the point. Back home, the jackal's wife asks how a jackal who can't fish came by a fish like that, and his answer in the verse is blunt: quarrels make people thin, and the otters' quarrel fed him. The tale's frame tells of a greedy monk who settled a dispute between two others over some robes, and kept the best one for himself. The jackal didn't have to fight or steal. The quarrel did the work for him. If the otters had split the fish themselves, even unevenly, each would have eaten well. A fair settlement made by the people involved keeps the fish whole.

segments.voice: Take a small quarrel that's still open, over chores, money, or who said what, and sit with both sides as a fair judge would, not the jackal. What's really yours, what's really theirs, and what's the middle being lost while the argument goes on? Breathe with it.
Quarrel. What fed the jackal, called in to judge between two otters fighting over their catch, who walked off with the middle himself. Today's word.
Your line: the judge ate the fish. Quarrels make people thin, the jackal says. Until tomorrow.

836.title: Two chariots
836.hook: two gods meet on a narrow road; the unrighteous won't yield and falls (Jataka 457)
836.howItsDone: Dhamma, the Pali form of the Sanskrit dharma, is one of the Three Jewels Buddhists take refuge in, together with the Buddha and the Sangha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two otters quarreled, and the jackal who judged walked off with the fish. Your line: the judge ate the fish. Today, a narrow road, high in the air.

Two chariots, nose to nose on a road with room for only one, and neither driver will back up. It could be any narrow lane on any weekday morning. In this Jataka tale the road runs through the sky, and the drivers are gods. One is named Dhamma, righteousness. The other is Adhamma, its opposite. Each has somewhere to be, and each expects the other to move.
screen: `A ROAD WITH ROOM FOR ONE.` → `TWO GODS, NOSE TO NOSE.` → `DHAMMA AND ADHAMMA.`

segments.voice: First, the meeting. In the tale, both gods travel through the world in their chariots, and one day their paths cross head on, where only one can pass. Second, the claims. Each tells the other to get out of the way, and each makes his case. Adhamma's case is force: he is strong, and gives way to no one. Dhamma's case is his goodness, and the honor the wise give it. Third, the refusal. Adhamma will not yield. Not an inch. He even offers to fight for the road. Dhamma's answer, in the tale's last verse between them, is that if Adhamma really is the stronger, he'll swallow the harsh words and make way for him. At the very moment Dhamma says it, Adhamma topples from his chariot headfirst, and the earth opens and swallows him. Fourth, the road goes on. Dhamma, the Bodhisatta in this tale, continues on his way. He never rams the other chariot or wins by shoving harder. The one who insists on never yielding is the one who falls, and the road opens for the one who was willing to give it up. Some readers find the whole point in that fall: what cannot bend at all eventually breaks. On an ordinary road, letting someone go first costs a few seconds; in a family argument, a little pride. The tale suggests refusing can cost a great deal more. Yielding here isn't weakness, and it isn't losing. It's how the road stays open.
screen: `TWO GODS, ONE NARROW ROAD.` · `EACH CLAIMS THE WAY.` · `ADHAMMA WILL NOT YIELD.` · `THE STUBBORN ONE FALLS.` · then, large: `YIELDING WINS.`

segments.voice: Find somewhere in the body that's braced, shoulders, jaw or hands: that's the body refusing to give way. Breathe out, and let it yield a little. Then picture one place you'll meet someone head on, a doorway, a merge on the road, a conversation that tends to dig in, and see yourself letting them go first.
Two chariots. A Jataka tale: righteousness and its opposite meet on a narrow road, and the one who will not yield is the one who falls. Today's word.
Your line: yielding wins. Adhamma never moved, and never got through. Day eight hundred thirty-six, done.

837.title: King Sivi's eyes
837.hook: a king gives his eyes to a blind beggar (Jataka 499)
837.howItsDone: The Sivi story is told in Buddhist teaching as an example of the perfection of giving (dana); everyday generosity takes smaller forms, like food offered to monastics, gifts to people in need, or time given freely.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two chariots on a narrow road, and the one who wouldn't give way was the one who fell. Your line: yielding wins. Today, a king who gives up far more than the road.

Some gifts cost nothing. Spare change, an old coat, a favor that fits the afternoon. King Sivi, in the Jataka, had given plenty of those: food, clothes, money, the story says, and he still wanted to give more. One day he made a quiet wish: if anyone ever asked for a part of his own body, he would give it. Then someone asked. A blind old man came before the king and asked for an eye.
screen: `GIFTS THAT COST NOTHING.` → `A KING'S QUIET WISH.` → `A BLIND MAN ASKS FOR AN EYE.`

segments.voice: First, the test. The blind man wasn't what he seemed. The Jataka says he was Sakka, king of the gods, in disguise, come to see whether Sivi meant his wish. Second, the cost. The king's ministers pleaded: give gold, give jewels, give anything, but not your eyes. Sivi sent for his surgeon anyway. The story doesn't hurry here. It dwells on the pain, and has the king say he gives not for gain but for the sake of awakening. Once the first eye was given, he gave the second. Third, the aftermath. Blind now, Sivi left the palace and sat alone by a pond. Sakka came back and asked him to speak the truth about his gift. The king said, truthfully, that he had given gladly. On those true words, the story says, his sight returned. Fourth, how to hold a story this extreme. It isn't a recipe for harming yourself. Tradition tells it as a picture of the perfection of giving, dana, stretched as far as it can go. Its question for an ordinary Tuesday is smaller and sharper: is there a gift that would actually cost you something? An hour you'd guarded. Credit you'd love to keep. An apology that bruises your pride. Sivi's tale isn't about the size of a gift. It's about giving past the part of you that would rather hold back.
screen: `A BEGGAR WHO WASN'T A BEGGAR.` · `GIVE GOLD, NOT YOUR EYES.` · `TRUE WORDS, AND SIGHT RETURNS.` · `A GIFT THAT COSTS YOU.` · then, large: `WHAT HE GAVE.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly what you could give that you'd rather keep: time, attention, a word of credit, patience with someone who wears yours thin. Don't pick the biggest answer; pick the one that's real. Then rest a while and simply notice the part of you that wants to hold on, without arguing with it.
Dana. Giving: the perfection King Sivi showed, a gift given whole, what he would most want to keep, asked for nothing back. Today's word.
Your line: what he gave. He gave it gladly, and asked nothing back. See you tomorrow.

838.title: The six-tusked elephant
838.hook: an elephant helps the hunter who wounded him cut his tusks (Jataka 514)
838.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers retell the Chaddanta story as a tale of patience and forgiveness; Buddhists practice letting go of resentment through reflection and loving-kindness meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dana, giving, and King Sivi, who gave both his eyes to a blind stranger. Your line: what he gave. Today, a gift given to an enemy.

The arrow comes from below. An elephant king walks a forest path, and a hunter hidden in a pit shoots a poisoned arrow up into him. In the Jataka this elephant is Chaddanta, the six-tusked, leader of a great herd. The story could end with him crushing the man in the pit. He has the strength to do it. It doesn't end that way.
screen: `AN ARROW FROM BELOW.` → `A HUNTER IN A PIT.` → `THE STRENGTH TO CRUSH HIM.`

segments.voice: It started small. Chaddanta had two wives, and one of them, Culla-subhadda, came to believe he favored the other. The slight, the story makes clear, was a shower of blossoms that fell on the wrong wife. She nursed it until she died wishing for revenge, and was reborn as a queen in a human kingdom. As queen, she sent a hunter named Sonuttara to find the elephant and bring back his tusks. He made the long journey and hid in a pit, wearing the yellow robe of a renunciant. Then the turn. Wounded, Chaddanta went for him, saw the robe, and stopped. He would not harm someone wearing that cloth, even as a trick. He asked the hunter why, heard about the queen, and understood who wanted him dead. The hunter tried to saw off the tusks and couldn't manage it. So Chaddanta took the saw in his own trunk, cut the tusks himself, handed them over, and died. Notice what the tale doesn't say. It doesn't say the wound didn't matter. It doesn't call the hunter good. It shows someone who had every right to strike back, and chose to help instead. When the queen saw the tusks, the story says, she remembered who he had been, and grief overwhelmed her. The grudge ran the whole story. The elephant is the one who stopped it.
screen: `A GRUDGE OVER FALLING BLOSSOMS.` · `A HUNTER IN A YELLOW ROBE.` · `HE STOPS, AND ASKS WHY.` · `THE SAW IN HIS OWN TRUNK.` · then, large: `HE HELPED THE HUNTER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small hurt, not the biggest one you carry: a sharp word, someone who took the credit. Find where it sits in the body, the jaw, the chest, the stomach, and without calling it fine, try setting it down for one breath, the way the elephant stopped at the sight of a robe. If it comes back, set it down again.
Chaddanta. The six-tusked elephant king who, wounded by a hunter, helped him take the tusks he came for. Today's word.
Your line: he helped the hunter. He had every right to strike back. Day eight hundred thirty-eight, done.

839.title: The man-eating king
839.hook: a prince keeps his word to return to a captor, and changes him (Jataka 537)
839.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Sutasoma story as an example of truthfulness (sacca), one of the ten perfections; keeping one's word is part of right speech in everyday practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chaddanta, the wounded elephant who cut his own tusks for the man who shot him. Your line: he helped the hunter. Today, a prisoner who walks back to his captor.

It starts with a promise to a stranger. A traveling brahmin arrives with verses to teach, and Prince Sutasoma tells him: wait here, I'll hear them when I come back from my bath. He never makes it back. On the road, a man who eats people snatches him and carries him into the forest. Now the prince has a promise he can't keep, and a captor with no reason to let him go.
screen: `A PROMISE TO A STRANGER.` → `SNATCHED ON THE ROAD.` → `A PROMISE HE CAN'T KEEP.`

segments.voice: The captor, the Jataka says, was once a king who acquired a taste for human flesh, was driven from his kingdom, and now lives in the forest as a man-eater. Carried off, Sutasoma weeps, and the man-eater mocks him for fearing death. That's not why I'm crying, the prince says. I made a promise to a brahmin and left it unkept. Let me go, and I'll keep it, and I'll come back. The man-eater lets him go, sure he'll never see him again. Sutasoma goes home, hears the verses, rewards the brahmin. His family begs him to stay. He goes back anyway, alone, to the man who plans to eat him. The man-eater is stunned. Who walks back to his own death to keep a word? He asks to hear the verses, and they're about the worth of keeping company with good people. He offers the prince a gift for each one. Among the gifts Sutasoma asks for: give up eating human flesh, and set your captives free. The man-eater agrees, and the captives go home. Nothing here is forced. No army, no trick. The captor is changed by watching someone keep a promise that cost him everything. Tradition reads it as a picture of sacca, truthfulness, one of the ten perfections.
screen: `A KING TURNED MAN-EATER.` · `HE WEEPS FOR A PROMISE.` · `HE WALKS BACK ALONE.` · `HE ASKS: STOP.` · then, large: `HE CAME BACK.`

Sacca. Truth, truthfulness: the perfection behind the man-eating king who let Prince Sutasoma go, never expecting him back, and was changed when he returned. Today's word.
Your line: he came back. A kept word did what a sword couldn't. That's day eight hundred thirty-nine.

840.title: The devoted son
840.hook: Sama cares for his blind parents and is shot by a king's arrow (Jataka 540)
840.tomorrow: The king who saw heaven and hell
840.howItsDone: Care for parents is part of everyday Buddhist ethics, and the Sama story is told as a picture of a child's devotion; some families make offerings in the names of parents, living and dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sacca, truthfulness, and Prince Sutasoma walking back to a man-eater to keep his word. Your line: he came back. Today ends the week, with a son at a river.

Early in the day, a young man kneels at a river to fill a water jar, and deer come down to drink beside him, unafraid. In the Jataka his name is Sama, and the water isn't for him. Back at the hut are his mother and father, both blind, who depend on him for everything. Somewhere in the trees, a king out hunting has already raised his bow.
screen: `A JAR AT THE RIVER.` → `DEER DRINK BESIDE HIM.` → `A KING RAISES HIS BOW.`

segments.voice: Sama's parents lived as forest ascetics, and the story says they lost their sight to a snake's venom. From then on, Sama was their eyes and hands: water, fruit, washing, a path kept clear. The king, Piliyakkha, sees a figure among the deer and shoots to bring him down, so he can ask who he is before he runs. The poison takes hold. Sama falls, and he doesn't ask for revenge. He asks who shot him and why, without anger. Then his thoughts turn to his parents. Who will bring them water now? The question undoes the king. He goes to the hut himself, tells the blind parents what he's done, and offers to serve them as their son did. Then comes truth again. His parents and a goddess who watched over him speak acts of truth, true words about Sama's goodness, and the poison leaves him. He rises and teaches the king. Look back over the last few days and the same shape keeps returning: Sivi's eyes, the elephant's tusks, the prince who came back, and now Sama at the river. Each time, someone with every reason to think of himself thinks first of someone else, and pays a price for it. Tradition pairs Sama with the perfection of kindness, metta.
screen: `HIS PARENTS' EYES AND HANDS.` · `AN ARROW AMONG THE DEER.` · `THE KING SERVES THEM INSTEAD.` · `TRUE WORDS, AND HE RISES.` · then, large: `THE DEVOTED SON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind whoever cared for you when you were small, a parent or anyone older who looked after you, living or gone, easy to love or not. Picture one ordinary thing they did for you that they never mentioned, and rest with it. If they've died, let this be a moment of remembering them well.
Sama. The devoted son who cared for his blind parents and, shot by a king, thought first of them. Today's word.
Your line: who will bring them water. Even as he fell, he thought of them first. Until tomorrow.

original.note: Pali Sama, the son's name; the tale is also called Suvannasama, golden Sama.

chat.says: In the Sama story, what does he say after the arrow hits him?
options: He asks why, without anger, then worries who will bring his parents water.
He curses the king and calls on the gods to punish him for it.
He begs the king to carry him to a healer in the city.
chat.meaning: Shot by the king, Sama asks why without anger and thinks first of his blind parents. That question changes the king.
